field_patches.after: This worked example uses one specified Euclidean SU(2) Weyl-doublet determinant family, the explicitly proved round index-one geometry, the central order-two test, and its mod-two-index bulk response. The finite BC2 calculation is a normalization check, not a continuum discretization or a general anomaly classification.

Assume AC. Let \(T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r\) and use the product Milnor model \(ET=(E_{S^1})^r\), \(BT=ET/T\), with right diagonal action \((e,x)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,t^{-1}\cdot x)\). For \(k\in\{\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}\), put \(A_T(k)=H^*(BT;k)\cong k[u_1,\ldots,u_r]\), where \(u_i=c_1(L_{\chi_i})\) is the degree-two class of the \(i\)th coordinate character line. For a smooth character \(\chi:T\to S^1\), set \(L_\chi=ET\times_T\mathbb C_\chi\), with the right equivalence \((e,z)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,\chi(t)^{-1}z)\). If \(\chi=\chi_{\mathbf n}\) for \(\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^r\), then \(c_1(L_\chi)=\sum_i n_i u_i\). Define \(\mathscr S_T(k)\) to consist of \(1\) and all finite products of \(c_1(L_\chi)\) for nontrivial characters \(\chi\). This is a multiplicative subset of \(A_T(k)\) with \(0\notin\mathscr S_T(k)\). For a topological space \(X\) with a continuous left \(T\)-action, set \(H_T^*(X;k)=H^*(ET\times_T X;k)\), with its \(A_T(k)\)-module structure induced by \(ET\times_T X\to BT\). For an \(A_T(k)\)-module \(N\), its localization \(\mathscr S_T(k)^{-1}N\) consists of fractions \(n/s\), with \(n\in N\), \(s\in\mathscr S_T(k)\), and \(n/s=n'/s'\) exactly when \(u(s'n-sn')=0\) for some \(u\in\mathscr S_T(k)\); addition is \((n/s)+(n'/s')=(s'n+sn')/(ss')\), and scalar multiplication is induced by the localized ring. The character-localized Borel equivariant cohomology is \(\mathscr S_T(k)^{-1}H_T^*(X;k)\). For \(r=0\), there are no nontrivial characters and \(\mathscr S_T(k)=\{1\}\).

field_patches.after: Let $\Gamma$ be the finite oriented boundary cycle of a square, with four edges $e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4$ and one plaquette. Use the compact matrix group $G=SU(2)=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-\overline b&\overline a\end{pmatrix}:a,b\in\mathbb C,\ |a|^2+|b|^2=1\right\}$ in its defining two-dimensional representation. Assign one link variable $U_j\in G$ to each edge and set the ordered plaquette holonomy to $U_p=U_1U_2U_3^{-1}U_4^{-1}$. The group is the unit sphere $S^3$ in the $(a,b)$ coordinates; let $\mu$ be its normalized round surface measure. For $\beta\ge0$, define the dimensionless action $S_\beta(U)=\beta\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}U_p\right)$ and partition function $Z_\beta=\int_{G^4}e^{-S_\beta(U)}\,d\mu^{\otimes4}(U)$. This finite graph integral satisfies $e^{-2\beta}\le Z_\beta\le1$, so it is finite and strictly positive. It has only four group variables and defines no continuum fields, no Wightman or Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction, and no Hamiltonian; it therefore does not solve the four-dimensional existence and mass-gap problem.

Let $\mathbb{H}$ be the real quaternion algebra with basis $1,i,j,k$, multiplication $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$, and norm $|a+bi+cj+dk|^2=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$. A Lie group is a finite-dimensional smooth manifold with smooth multiplication and inversion; its Lie algebra is its tangent space at the identity with the bracket induced by left-invariant vector fields. Let $SU(2)$ be the group of unit quaternions and $SO(3)$ the group of linear maps of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb{H}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{i,j,k\}\cong\mathbb R^3$ preserving the Euclidean inner product and having determinant $+1$. A Lie algebra is simple if it is nonabelian and has no nonzero proper ideals. For this example, a compact simple gauge group means a compact connected Lie group with a simple Lie algebra. Its global form means the Lie group itself, including its central quotient, rather than only its Lie algebra. The kernel of a group homomorphism is the inverse image of the identity, and the center is the set of elements commuting with every group element. The map $\pi:SU(2)\to SO(3)$ defined by $\pi(q)x=qxq^{-1}$ is a surjective homomorphism with kernel $\{1,-1\}$; its differential identifies the simple Lie algebras of $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$, while the groups are distinct. Therefore, a proof of a claim quantified over every compact simple gauge group at $SU(2)$ alone does not discharge the separate $SO(3)$ case.

For every compact connected finite-dimensional Lie group $G$ whose Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is nonabelian and has no nonzero proper Lie ideals, construct a nontrivial four-dimensional quantum Yang–Mills theory with gauge group $G$. A Lie group is a smooth manifold with smooth multiplication and inversion, and its Lie algebra is its tangent space at the identity with the bracket induced by left-invariant vector fields. A Wightman realization means a theory satisfying the Wightman axioms: it supplies a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, a unitary representation of translations and proper, orthochronous Lorentz isometries of Minkowski space $\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-,+,+,+)$, and local quantum fields as operator-valued tempered distributions on Schwartz test functions acting on a common dense invariant domain. The fields transform covariantly; gauge-invariant fields localized in regions whose points are spacelike separated, meaning $\eta(x-y,x-y)>0$, commute. Correlation functions are the vacuum expectation distributions of finite products of smeared fields. The self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ generating time translations has spectrum $\sigma(H)\subseteq[0,\infty)$, and there is a unique Poincaré-invariant vacuum vector $\Omega$ up to phase with $H\Omega=0$. Alternatively, a Euclidean construction gives Schwinger distributions, meaning Euclidean vacuum correlation distributions on $\mathbb R^4$, satisfying the Osterwalder–Schrader axioms (temperedness, Euclidean covariance, reflection positivity, permutation symmetry, and clustering) strongly enough for reconstruction of a Wightman theory. The required nontrivial gauge content includes local operator fields corresponding to gauge-invariant local polynomials in a smooth connection's curvature and its covariant derivatives, with short-distance correlations prescribed in a specified construction by asymptotic freedom (the perturbative prediction that the gauge coupling tends to zero at short distances) and perturbative renormalization. It includes a local stress-energy tensor whose charges generate spacetime translations and an operator product expansion, meaning a short-distance expansion of products of local fields in local fields. Here the curvature of a smooth local connection $A$ is $F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A\wedge A]$, and its covariant derivative on adjoint-valued forms is $D_A=d+[A,\cdot]$. The required mass gap is a finite number $\Delta>0$ such that $\sigma(H)\cap(0,\Delta)=\varnothing$, using units $c=\hbar=1$. Confinement is a separate question and is not part of this problem.

$$[U]_D:=-\frac14 I_D(U),\qquad [Y]_F:=\frac12 I_F(Y).$$

A Hermitian conjugate in a physical F action means the conjugate of the extracted coefficient, added once. It does not mean replacing that operation by an unadjusted raw ordered antichiral integral. Physical chiral component names are fixed by

$$\Phi(y,\theta)=\phi(y)+\sqrt2\theta^\alpha\psi_\alpha(y)+2\theta^1\theta^2F(y),\qquad y=x+i\theta\sigma\bar\theta.$$

Thus the earlier mathematical components satisfy $\psi_{\mathrm{raw},\alpha}=\sqrt2\psi_\alpha$ and $F_{\mathrm{raw}}=2F$, while $\phi$ is unchanged. A component variation means coefficient extraction followed by this fixed conversion; it is not a rescaling of an integrated quantum field. Dimensions remain $[\phi]=1$, $[\psi]=3/2$, $[F]=2$.

The anti-automorphism gives $(\theta^1\theta^2F_{\mathrm{raw}})^*=-\bar\theta^{\dot1}\bar\theta^{\dot2}\bar F_{\mathrm{raw}}$. The scalar term of the raw D integral is $4\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\bar\phi\partial_\nu\phi$ after compact-support integration by parts; the physical bracket gives $-\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\bar\phi\partial_\nu\phi$. These identities specify why the raw and physical component notations cannot be identified. Physical component potentials and coupling coefficients use the physical names above.

At fixed chiral coordinates define $P_{\mathrm{raw}}=\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot2}}\partial^L_{\bar\theta^{\dot1}}|_{\bar\theta=0}=\bar D_{\dot2}\bar D_{\dot1}$. With $\epsilon_{12}=1$ and inverse $\epsilon^{12}=-1$, one has $\bar D^{\dot\alpha}\bar D_{\dot\alpha}=-2P_{\mathrm{raw}}$ and $\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\bar D^{\dot\alpha}=2P_{\mathrm{raw}}$. $$[U]_D=[P_{\mathrm{phys}}U]_F,\qquad P_{\mathrm{phys}}=-\frac12P_{\mathrm{raw}}=\frac14\bar D^{\dot\alpha}\bar D_{\dot\alpha}=-\frac14\bar D_{\dot\alpha}\bar D^{\dot\alpha}.$$

The order of contracted barred derivatives is therefore always part of a one-quarter projection formula. The identities follow directly by coefficient extraction and nilpotent coordinate translation, whose extra spacetime terms are total derivatives. They assert no boundary cancellation without that hypothesis.

$$
S_0[\phi]=\mathcal I\!\left[-\frac12\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi-\frac12m^2\phi^2-\frac{g}{4!}\phi^4\right],\qquad \mathcal O_6=\phi^2\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi,
$$

with $S_\epsilon=S_0+\epsilon(C/\Lambda^2)\mathcal I(\mathcal O_6)$. After specializing $M_s=m$, the leading Euler derivative is $\mathcal E_0=\Box\phi-m^2\phi-(g/6)\phi^3$. In $\widehat{\mathcal Q}_6$,

$$
[\mathcal O_6]= -\frac{1}{3}[M_s^2\phi^4]-\frac{g}{18}[\phi^6].
$$

The identity-leading local change of variables $\phi\mapsto\phi+\epsilon C\phi^3/(3\Lambda^2)$ transforms the action through this order to

$$
S_\epsilon\!\left[\phi+\epsilon\frac{C\phi^3}{3\Lambda^2}\right] = S_0[\phi]-\epsilon\frac{Cm^2}{3\Lambda^2}\mathcal I(\phi^4)-\epsilon\frac{Cg}{18\Lambda^2}\mathcal I(\phi^6).
$$

The mass spurion gives each term in the quotient identity weight six. Give the formal coefficient $\Lambda^{-1}$ weight $-1$; multiplying the identity by $C/\Lambda^2$ then places every term in a finite weight-four action-density space, and $F[\phi]\mathcal E_0$ lies in that space for $F[\phi]=-C\phi^3/(3\Lambda^2)$. The map uses the convention $\Psi(\phi)=\phi-\epsilon F[\phi]$, and $\epsilon F$ has the units of $\phi$. This is a formal scalar-action calculation under the stated boundary convention; it asserts neither a physical realization nor an on-shell scattering result.
